items.section_heading: Kabaddi - I. Answer the following Questions
items.stem: List the landmarks in the history of Kabaddi in India.
items.answer: The main landmarks are: the game was demonstrated for the first time at the international level during 1936 in Berlin Olympics by Hanuman Vyayam Pracharak Mandal, Amravati, Maharashtra; it was introduced in the Indian Olympic Games at Calcutta in 1938; in 1950 the All India Kabaddi Federation came into existence and compiled standard rules; the Amateur Kabaddi Federation of India (AKFI) was founded in 1973; the Asian Kabaddi Federation (AKF) was founded in 1978; and the Kabaddi World Cup was first played in 2004, then in 2007 and 2010.
grounding: The game was demonstrated for the first time at the international level during 1936 in Berlin Olympics by Hanuman Vyayam Pracharak Mandal, Amravati, Maharashtra.
The game was introduced in the Indian Olympic Games at Calcutta in 1938.
In 1950, the All India Kabaddi Federation came into existence and compiled standard rules.
The Amateur Kabaddi Federation of India (AKFI) was founded in 1973.
The Asian Kabaddi Federation (AKF) was founded in 1978.
The Kabaddi World Cup was first played in 2004, then in 2007 and 2010.

items.section_heading: Kabaddi - I. Answer the following Questions
items.stem: What is the system of scoring in Kabaddi?
items.answer: One point score will be given to each team for every opponent who is deemed out. If a team makes all the players of the opponent team out, that team is entitled to get 2 points as a bonus, and this is known as Lona. One point is also awarded to the raider when they cross the bonus line. The team which scores the highest number of points at the end of the match is declared the winner.
grounding: One point score will be given to each team for every opponent who is deemed out.
And if your team, makes all the players of your opponent team out, your team is entitled to get 2 points as a bonus. This is known as Lona.
One point shall be awarded to the raider when they cross the bonus line.
The team which scores the highest number of points at the end of the match shall be declared the winner.

items.section_heading: Kabaddi - I. Answer the following Questions
items.stem: What are the rules regarding substitutions?
items.answer: The rules are: (i) five reserve players can be substituted with the permission of the referee during time out or interval; (ii) substituted players can be re-substituted; (iii) if any player is suspended or disqualified from the match, no substitution is allowed for that particular player and the team plays with less number of players; (iv) no substitution is allowed during the official time out; and (v) substitution is not allowed for players who are deemed out.
grounding: Five reserve players can be substituted with the permission of the referee during time out or interval.
Substituted players can be re-substituted.
If any player is suspended or disqualified from the match, no substitution is allowed for that particular player. The team will play with less number of players.
No substitution is allowed during the official time out.
Substitution is not allowed for players who are deemed out.

items.section_heading: Kabaddi - I. Answer the following Questions
items.stem: What is a bonus point?
items.answer: A bonus point is the one point that shall be awarded to the raider when they cross the bonus line. The bonus line is applicable only when there are a minimum of 6 players in the court. The raider has to cross the bonus line to score the bonus point before touching the antis or before he is caught by the antis. If the raider while crossing the bonus line is caught, then a point will be awarded to the defending team instead. There shall be no revival for bonus points.

items.section_heading: Judo - I. Answer the following Questions
items.stem: Briefly list the typical characteristics of Judo?
items.answer: Judo is a popular martial art, combative and Olympic sport. It was developed in Japan in the late 19th century by using the principles of balance and leverage adapted from jujutsu. Its most prominent feature is its competitive element: the objective is either to throw or putdown the opponent to the ground, to immobilise or otherwise subdue the opponent with a grappling maneuver, or to force the opponent to submit by joint locking or by executing a stranglehold or choke. Strikes and thrusts by hands and feet as well as self-defense are a part of judo. Many are trained in judo either for participation in competition or for self-defense.
grounding: Judo is a popular martial art, combative and Olympic sport.

items.section_heading: Wrestling - I. Answer the following Questions
items.stem: List the landmarks in the history of wrestling in India?
items.answer: Wrestling in India then was popularly known as Malla Yuddha, and it received regular patronage from the Emperors and Kings. In the famous Indian epic Mahabharata, Bhima was considered to be a great wrestler of that time and other great wrestlers included Jarasandha, Duryodhana and Karna. Even during the British rule wrestling in India got encouraging support, as the British rulers included the game into the military practice. India was considered among the top 10 countries in wrestling till the 1960s and hosted the World Wrestling Championship at New Delhi in 1967. In the Olympic Games the first medal was won by K.D. Jadhav in 1952 at Helsinki Games, and in 2008 Sushil Kumar brought a second bronze medal for India at the Beijing Olympic Games.

items.section_heading: Wrestling - I. Answer the following Questions
items.stem: List and describe the scoring rules and terms of wrestling.
items.answer: The scoring rules and terms of wrestling are: (i) Takedown - it occurs when a man takes the opponent to the mat from a standing position; this is worth one point, but can be worth more if the opponent is brought down onto his back. (ii) Exposure - it is turning an opponent, and once the line of the back area breaks a 90-degree angle, points are scored; this can occur both from the feet and on the mat, and a wrestler who holds his opponent in a danger position for five seconds will receive one extra point. (iii) Reversal - when a wrestler comes to the top position in control, he has scored a reversal, worth one point. (iv) Escape - when an athlete works to come out from the bottom position, after being under dominant control, and gets to their feet facing the rival, the athlete has then scored an escape, worth one point. (v) Fall - bringing two shoulders of the opponent on the ground. On the points table, 1 point is for holding of the opponent on the ground, 2 points for placing the opponent in danger and 3 points for bringing the opponent into immediate danger position.
